title: When family pushes back
hook: They might be hurt, scared or angry. You can stay kind and stay Muslim at the same time.

screens.text: Maybe it's a cold silence, a long argument, or "this is just a phase." When family pushes back, it hurts, especially from the people who raised you. Today: how to stay steady and kind, without giving up your faith or your family.
**What's usually underneath.** Most pushback is fear, not hate [Field Guide ch. 4]. When you hear the fear under the words, it's easier not to take every sharp sentence as an attack.

screens.title: What they say, and the fear underneath

cards.back: Fear of losing you: the person they raised and thought they knew.
Fear of what they've seen on the news about Muslims.
Fear of what relatives will say.
Fear that someone pressured you into it.

screens.text: **Two things at once.** The Qur'an tells you to treat your parents well, and not to obey them if they push you to worship anything besides Allah [Q 29:8]. Even then: keep them company in this world *with kindness* [Q 31:14–15].
bubbles: So the line is clear: **stay Muslim, stay kind.** You don't have to choose.

screens.prompt: Stay Muslim, stay kind. Which of these fit?

items.text: Keep praying, even if they don't like it
items.why: You don't leave your faith for anyone [Q 29:8].

items.text: Give up Islam to keep the peace
items.why: You don't obey anyone in leaving the worship of Allah [Q 29:8]. Kindness, yes; giving up your faith, no.

items.text: Cut them off until they accept it
items.why: The Qur'an asks you to keep them company with kindness, even when they disagree [Q 31:14–15].

items.text: Keep showing up for birthdays, dinners and calls
items.why: That's the kindness part, and it speaks louder than any argument.
Respect goes both ways. No mocking their faith.

screens.prompt: Hannah's dad says, "You've been brainwashed. You're throwing away how we raised you." What's the best first response?

options.text: "I know this is hard, Dad. I'm still me, and I love you. Can we talk about it when we're both calmer?"
options.feedback: Yes. It names his feelings, reassures him, and avoids a fight in the heat of the moment.
Not quite. Even if true, it pours fuel on the fire. Lead with love first.

options.text: Walk out and stop speaking to him
options.feedback: Not quite. A break to cool off is fine, but cutting him off goes against the kindness Islam asks [Q 31:14–15].

steps.text: **Don't debate in the heat.** Say, "Let's talk later," and mean it.
**Show, don't argue.** More patient, more helpful, more honest: that speaks louder than any argument.
**Keep showing up:** birthdays, dinners, phone calls.
**Give it time.** Many families soften over months, and relationships often end up better than before [Yaqeen 2025].

screens.character: An upset parent. They love their child but feel hurt and scared, and they've heard negative things about Islam. They can be sharp and emotional, but never abusive, threatening or insulting.
screens.setup: A week after you told them you're Muslim, your mom (or dad) brings it up again at dinner: "I've been thinking about this, and I'm not okay with it."
screens.goal: Stay calm and kind, show you still love them, answer briefly without debating, and leave the door open.
screens.success_looks_like: You acknowledge their feelings, reassure them you're still their child, don't argue theology, set a calmer time to talk, and end warmly.
screens.coach_notes: The parent pushes on: 'It's a phase', 'You were raised Christian', 'They'll make you cover up / marry someone', 'What will Grandma say?', 'Are you safe?'. They soften when the convert listens and reassures, and get sharper if lectured. Debrief: one moment the convert stayed calm, one sentence to try next time, and a reminder that this conversation will happen more than once.

screens.text: **Respect goes both ways.** Allah doesn't forbid you from being good and fair to people who don't fight you over your faith [Q 60:8]. Honor their beliefs too: no mocking their faith, no lectures at Christmas dinner.
bubbles: Asma' kept close ties with her mother, who wasn't Muslim, with the Prophet's blessing ﷺ [Bukhari 2620].

screens.title: When it's more than words
screens.intro: If you're threatened, hurt, locked out or told to leave, that's not "pushback." Your safety comes first.

steps.text: {teen}Under 18? Stay respectful and avoid standoffs. If you're told not to pray, don't fight it out alone: talk to {{mentor.name}}.{/teen}

chips: My parents won't let me pray at home. What do I do?
They say I'll go to hell for leaving their religion.
How do I explain Islam without starting a fight?
My family won't talk to me anymore.

screens.text: One small kindness for your family today.
steps: Do one kind thing: a call, a text, help with something, a meal together
screens.optional_extra: Make a du'a for your family by name, in your own words.

screens.text: Stay Muslim, stay kind. Hear the fear under the anger, don't debate in the heat, and keep showing up.
Families take time. Your kindness is planting something.

prayerPhrase.meaning: Guide us to the straight path
prayerPhrase.when: Al-Fatiha, line 5 (after Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in). You ask for guidance in every rak'ah, for yourself and the people you love. [Q 1:6]

check.prompt: Your parent pushes you to give up Islam. What does the Qur'an ask of you?

options.text: Don't obey them in that, but keep treating them with kindness
Obey them to keep the peace
options.feedback: Not quite. You don't leave your faith for anyone, but you stay kind to them [Q 31:14–15].

options.text: Cut them off until they accept it
options.feedback: Not quite. The Qur'an asks you to keep them company with kindness, even when they disagree [Q 31:14–15].

check.prompt: An argument about your faith is heating up. What's the best move?

options.text: Reassure them and suggest talking later, when it's calmer
options.feedback: Right. Heat rarely changes minds; patience and kindness often do.

options.text: Keep going until you've proven your point
options.feedback: Not quite. Winning the argument can lose the relationship. Pause, and come back to it.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Don't obey parents in leaving the worship of Allah alone, but keep them company in this world with kindness [Q 31:14–15; Q 29:8]. Excellence to parents [Q 17:23–24].
- Allah doesn't forbid kindness and justice to those who don't fight you over religion [Q 60:8].
- Asma' and her mother [Bukhari 2620].
- Family pushback is usually fear; families often come around with time [Field Guide ch. 4]. Parental relationships typically dip at disclosure and recover, often better than before [Yaqeen 2025]. Family is a top convert pain point; some converts are forbidden to pray at home [Research Notes - Retention and Convert Voices, V1, V10, V19].

**Likely questions**
- *"Not allowed to pray at home."* Respond with care; quiet, private prayer in their own room; for minors, route to the mentor and imam; escalate.
- *"They say I'll go to hell."* Don't argue about anyone's afterlife; suggest replying with love ("I know you say that because you care about me"); no predictions (Spec §6.2 rule 9).
- *"How do I explain without a fight?"* One or two sentences about what Islam means to them personally; invite questions later; Day 28 has more.
- *"They won't talk to me."* Validate grief; keep the door open (a birthday text, a note); be patient; mentor support.
- *"They want me at church / Christmas."* Holiday module and Q5: keep ties and attend family gatherings; skip religious rites; ask the imam. Don't resolve the greeting question.

**Escalate:** any threat, violence, being thrown out or cut off (crisis resources first: 911, National Domestic Violence Hotline 1-800-799-7233, 988; offer to alert their chosen person); a minor forbidden to practice; holiday questions (Q5); a non-Muslim spouse (Q21).

**Don't**
- Don't encourage cutting off family, or coach a minor to deceive or defy parents (Spec §6.2 rule 12).
- Don't disparage the family's religion.
- Don't quote the "awliya" verse that Spec Q19 sets aside; teach kindness and justice instead (Q19).

**Role-play brief:** A loving but upset parent, a week after the news. Sharp at times ("It's a phase", "They'll make you marry someone", "What will Grandma say?"), never abusive or threatening. Softens with warmth and listening; hardens with lecturing. The convert sees a "stop role-play" button. Debrief: one calm moment, one better phrase, and the reminder that this is a long conversation.
